articles.title: Trump se revolta ao ser questionado sobre uso de arma nuclear no Irã: 'Que pergunta estúpida' | G1
articles.standfirst: No último domingo, os dois países voltaram a trocar agressões pela primeira vez desde julho. Republicano voltou a dizer que Teerã está derrotada militarmente, apesar da continuidade dos bombardeios e de os EUA não terem cumprido seus objetivos iniciais na guerra.
articles.summary: No último domingo, os dois países voltaram a trocar agressões pela primeira vez desde julho. Republicano voltou a dizer que Teerã está derrotada militarmente, apesar da continuidade dos bombardeios e de os EUA não terem cumprido seus objetivos iniciais na guerra.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , se irritou com um repórter nesta segunda-feira (31) ao ser questionado por uma repórter se ele cogitaria usar uma arma nuclear para atacar o Irã.

"Não há motivo nenhum para isso. Que pergunta estúpida, na verdade. Eles estão aí, totalmente derrotados militarmente. Então, não. Eu os derroto e deveria usar uma arma nuclear?! Que pergunta estúpida", respondeu Trump.

Apesar de declarar vitória repetidamente no conflito, Trump não cumpriu boa parte dos objetivos traçados desde o início da guerra contra Teerã, iniciada por uma ação em conjunto dos EUA e de Israel.

Nesta segunda, Trump disse que as Forças Armadas americanas voltarão a realizar "fortes ataques" contra o Irã em breve: "Vamos acertá-los com força", afirmou Trump à emissora norte-americana Fox News.

O ataque, segundo Trump, será em resposta ao bombardeio iraniano feito no domingo (30) contra bases dos EUA na Jordânia — que por sua vez foi uma retaliação a uma agressão dos EUA contra a ilha de Larak (leia mais abaixo) .

O Irã, por outro lado, mandou sinais contraditórios nesta segunda-feira. O presidente iraniano, Masoud Pezeshkian, afirmou que o país ainda busca uma solução negociada para o conflito com os EUA e que quer retomar as tratativas, enquanto uma autoridade do país prometeu à agência de notícias Reuters amplas retaliações a qualquer agressão dos EUA.

Donald Trump responde a perguntas da imprensa durante evento no Salão Oval da Casa Branca, em 31 de agosto de 2026 — Foto: Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters

No domingo (30), os dois países voltaram a trocar agressões pela primeira vez desde julho.

O Comando Central dos EUA afirmou que realizou uma ação "limitada e precisa" contra forças iranianas que instalavam minas na região. Segundo a pasta, os alvos representavam uma "ameaça iminente".

O Irã retaliou lançando mísseis contra bases militares dos EUA na Jordânia. Segundo Washington, todos os projéteis foram interceptados por defesas aéreas, menos um deles, que caiu em uma área não habitada.

O Exército iraniano também afirmou ter atacado a base aérea de Al Minhad, nos Emirados Árabes Unidos, durante a madrugada desta segunda-feira. O governo dos Emirados, porém, negou a informação.

A retomada dos ataques ocorreu após semanas de aumento da pressão econômica dos EUA contra o Irã e seus parceiros comerciais . O governo Trump ampliou as sanções econômicas contra Teerã e passou a priorizar medidas financeiras em vez de novas ações militares.

Trump ainda não alcançou os objetivos que estabeleceu no início da guerra. Entre eles estão desmantelar o programa nuclear iraniano, limitar a capacidade do país de atacar seus rivais regionais e criar condições para que os iranianos derrubem o governo dos líderes religiosos.

articles.title: Interior designers say these home decor choices will still look good in 10 years
articles.summary: From warm colors to natural materials, these expert-approved ideas have staying power.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

Design trends swing like a pendulum. Not long ago, homes were filled with shiplap, cool gray interiors and minimalist designs. Now, maximalism and bolder hues are back. While fads can be fun, thoughtful decorating choices can help your home feel current for years to come.

Timeless interiors are thoughtfully assembled — not just thrown together. "I was always told that you should pick hard materials (such as countertops and flooring) that you know you'll like for at least 10 years, and I think the same goes for large furniture pieces," explains lead Home Editor Jessica Dodell-Feder . "Don't buy a trendy bed frame! But trendy throw pillows, sheets or rugs? Sure!"

I asked interior designers which colors, materials and decorating choices have lasting appeal.

When done right, Mimi Meacham, principal designer and owner of Marian Louise Design , says neutrals "create a calm backdrop that lets the architecture, furnishings, and the people living in the home shine." Trade bright whites and cool gray interiors for more lived-in hues. Meacham says you can't go wrong with earthy beiges, soft taupes and creamy ivories.

Light and bright isn't the only way. Sarah Kuchar, interior designer and owner of Kuchar Studio in Chicago, says moodier, saturated hues can also "behave like neutrals rather than statements." Ground spaces with burgundies, chocolate browns and oxbloods, then layer in softer neutrals like warm whites and earthy terracotta. The key, according to Kuchar? "Warmth used with restraint."

Sprinkle in trending colors, like Grounded, the mossy olive named Behr's 2027 Color of the Year , as accents. "I usually recommend using those in smaller doses — through textiles, art or accessories — rather than committing to them on permanent elements like cabinetry or tile," Meacham adds.

Better Homes & Gardens Adlin Storage Bench

Not a fan of recessed cans and flush fixtures? You're not alone. "Layered lighting makes a space feel warm, inviting, relaxed and lived in. It changes the entire mood of a room in a way that overhead lighting just can't," says designer and Survivor winner Kim Wolfe , who stars on HGTV's Rock the Block .

Ambient lighting is the answer to your "big light" woes . "Classic silhouettes always win," adds Meacham. Think: "lanterns, tailored sconces and simple chandeliers with clean lines."

Better Homes & Gardens Glass Portable Lamp

Borrow from nature's palette and it's hard to go wrong. "It feels restorative no matter where you put it, whether it's through a paint color or a pillow pattern," says Meredith McKenzie, principal designer at The Selective Design in Macon, Ga.

Soft blues and subdued greens are a natural fit for bedrooms since they "promote a sense of tranquility," but McKenzie argues that green, in particular, is one of the most versatile colors to work with. "Recently green was identified as a 'new neutral' in the design world, but to so many of us designers, it's not a new idea," she jokes, adding that it "feels effortless because you can pair it with anything."

Threshold Medium Blue Painted Ceramic Vase

Invest in quality materials that "age rather than simply wear out," says Rozit Arditi, principal designer and founder of Arditi Design in New York City. Patina is the whole point here — white oak turns honey gold, full-grain leather softens, unlacquered brass darkens and other natural materials slowly change over time, which designers agree contributes to their overall staying power. "I don't necessarily see these changes as imperfections, but more of what gives a material character and longevity," adds Arditi.

"One material I'll never tire of is marble," says Meacham. "Natural stone has variation and movement that simply can't be replicated, and that's what makes it feel timeless."

Designers recommend taking a slow and steady approach when decorating. "The homes that stand the test of time are the ones that feel collected over decades — not furnished all at once," says Meacham. Fill your space with family heirlooms, flea market finds and other carefully collected pieces that speak to you, rather than the trends. "I think the best way to choose pieces that feel timeless is to buy things you truly love — then you won't care if it's 'in style' or not," adds Dodell-Feder.

Have an eye for antiques? "They've already stood the test of time, which is the best proof there is," says designer Annie Meyers-Shyer, author of This Oak House . "Dark wood tones, lots of detail, very traditional" pieces will go the distance.

articles.title: 'Run, Run, Run': Grand Canyon flood survivor recounts race to safety
articles.summary: "It was like something out of a movie," survivor Scott Svedin said.
articles.body:
Survivors of a deadly flash flood that swept through the floor of the Grand Canyon over the weekend described a horrific escape as they ran through rising muddy water in a desperate effort to reach higher ground.

Gabriel Bergemann and David Gregory told ABC News that they were backpacking together at the bottom of the national park on Saturday afternoon when disaster struck, and park rangers told them to run across a footbridge over a raging creek to higher ground.

Bergemann said that 10 minutes after crossing the bridge, a wall of water came through and washed it away.

"If they hadn't told us to evacuate when they did, I think a lot of people wouldn't have made it," he told ABC News.

Gregory added that the water level in the creek they crossed seemed to be "getting bigger and bigger as more water was coming into the creek."

"I was just thinking that if someone fell into the creek, I don't know how they would be able to get out," he said.

Grand Canyon National Park Service officials said on Monday that a second body had been recovered from the flooded area. A search continued for more than a dozen people who remain missing or unaccounted for.

One of the individuals missing was earlier identified as Texas chiropractor Dr. John Giusti in a message posted on Facebook by Whipple City Family Chiropractic in New York, according to ABC affiliate WFAA . Giusti's family confirmed that he was among the dead on Monday.

Giusti, who worked for ChiroHabit in Granbury, Texas, was a former partner at Whipple City Family Chiropractic, which posted a message on Facebook from Giusti's wife, who said he was with a hiking group when the flash flood swept through the area where they were camping. In her message, Giusti's wife described him as a "deeply loved husband, father and pillar of our family."

More than 60 people, most of them hikers and campers, were air evacuated from Grand Canyon's Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail on Saturday, according to park officials.

The flood hit around 2:30 p.m. local time in the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch areas of the Grand Canyon amid a monsoonal downpour that produced "a significant flash-flood event," officials said.

Erica Viola and her husband, Scott Svedin, told ABC News they were camping at Bright Angel Campground when they were told to evacuate immediately.

"This was something out of a movie," said Svedin, who described struggling through knee-high water and mud to reach safety.

Viola added, "We just heard people yell, 'Run, Run, Run.' And there's 40 of us running through this deep muddy water trying to make it to the bridge."

Viola said that once she and Svedin got across the footbridge, it was destroyed by the torrent of floodwater that turned the creek they had crossed into a raging river.

"Once we got to the bridge, that's when this 15-foot wall of water came through the campground at Phantom Ranch and just wiped out all the bridges in the creek," Viola said.

Viola said that she lost most of her belongings in the flooding.

The Grand Canyon National Park Service (NPS) said in a statement on Sunday that the flooding caused extensive damage to infrastructure in the inner canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, which supplies water from the canyon for use in the park.

"The flash flood resulted in significant impacts to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon. Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, eliminating hiker access across the creek," the Grand Canyon NPS said.

The Grand Canyon NPS said the Transcanyon Waterline is currently not operational, leaving the entire park with limited water reserves. As a result, all overnight guest lodging and concessions inside the park have been halted.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Giusti's name and his most recent employer.

articles.title: 'Justice 4 HeeHaw': Cedartown farm owner mourning loss of beloved baby donkey allegedly shot, killed by officer
articles.summary: It was unusually quiet at Elsberry Farm in Cedartown on Monday afternoon.  For Elsberry Farm owner Hannah Israel, who bottle-raised HeeHaw as if he was her o...
articles.body:
It was unusually quiet at Elsberry Farm in Cedartown on Monday afternoon.

You could hear the cows, the pigs and the roosters.

That's because HeeHaw, the beloved donkey who had become a fixture at the farm, was allegedly shot and killed by a Cedartown Police officer early Sunday morning while the officer was searching for a missing child.

For Elsberry Farm owner Hannah Israel, who bottle-raised HeeHaw as if he was her own from the time he was just an hour old, the silence is heartbreaking.

"He was my kid," Israel said. "I bottle raised him from one hour old, and I was up at all hours of the night."

HeeHaw had no problem making himself heard.

"He would normally be standing right over there talking while I'm talking because he thought he could talk like a person could talk," Israel said.

And apparently, he considered just about everyone a friend.

"Every time he saw somebody, he would run up and bray," Israel said. "And then do a really goofy sound, and because he loved people, and he thought he was a person. He slept in my bed for the first three months of his life."

That friendly personality may have been what ultimately put HeeHaw in harm's way.

Cedartown Police Chief Jamie Newsom said one of his officers shot and killed the donkey while officers were searching for a missing child.

"That search took them to the incident location where this very unfortunate and heartbreaking event occurred," Newsom said.

Newsom declined to provide details about what happened immediately before the shooting, saying the incident is now under investigation.

He did confirm that body camera footage exists and that he has reviewed it.

"I will confirm body cam video exists. I have viewed it, but I won't comment as to what it portrays to respect the investigation that that state agency is going to do so," Newsom said.

The Georgia Department of Agriculture's Law Enforcement Division was at Elsberry Farm on Monday investigating HeeHaw's death.

Israel said she is struggling to understand how the situation ended with the loss of an animal who was such a major part of her daily life.

"I don't see any reason that he is not here right now," she said.

Newsom said he understands the heartbreak.

"They're members of the human family, and I am too, and heartbroken," he said.

For Israel, the loss is more than the death of a farm animal.

HeeHaw had been with her through countless days and nights since she raised him from infancy. He followed her around, greeted people and, by all accounts, made sure nobody visiting the farm left without hearing his opinion.

Now, the farm has cows, pigs and roosters -- but one very important voice is missing.

"Just traumatized and shocked," Israel said. "I honestly can't even believe he's not here. He was such a part of our lives, just daily, every single day. Yeah, there's no words."

The Georgia Department of Agriculture investigation remains ongoing. Authorities have not released additional details about what led to the shooting.

articles.title: Teen girl who recorded San Diego mosque shooting livestream is charged with murder
articles.summary: According to the indictment, the North Carolina teen agreed before the attack that she would record the livestream, distribute it and release a document written by the attackers.
articles.body: A 17-year-old North Carolina girl who recorded a livestream of a shooting that killed three people at a San Diego mosque and disseminated the attackers’ white supremacist writings has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting, a district attorney said Monday. Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O’Neill said at a news conference in Winston-Salem that the girl, identified in court records as Sarah Lindsey Santiago, was arrested last week. A grand jury indicted her on three counts of murder and one count of conspiracy Monday. Santiago’s attorney did not immediately return a message from The Associated Press seeking comment Monday. Under North Carolina law, the aiding-and-abetting charges carry the same penalties as if the girl had committed the attack herself, O’Neill said. According to the indictment, Santiago agreed prior to the attack that she would record the livestream, distribute it and release a document written by the attackers. She carried out those tasks, it said, and she purchased a patch bearing a white supremacist symbol and sent it to one of the gunmen to wear during the attack. “The individual here, locally, was the person who was recording the livestream,” O’Neill said. “She disseminated that information and she published their manifesto.” Cain Clark, 17, and Caleb Vazquez, 18, stormed the Islamic Center on May 18 before being driven back outside by a security guard who exchanged gunfire with them as he initiated a lockdown, helping to protect 140 children who were just steps away. The pair killed the guard, Amin Abdullah, and two other men before taking their own lives in a vehicle nearby. They left behind rambling writings full of vitriol against a wide range of people, and cited the shooter who killed 51 people at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 2019, as one of their models for their violence. The two also planned subsequent attacks on two other targets: a Jewish temple and a predominantly Black high school, O’Neill said. He credited the guard and other victims at the mosque with having saved countless lives. The attackers’ writings cited a range of far-right ideological inspirations, including the notion that white people are being replaced by other populations, and detailed their motives and goals. They included hateful rhetoric toward Jewish people, Muslims and Islam, as well as the LGBTQ+ community, Black people, women and the political left and right. They indicated they were trying to accelerate the collapse of society. Vazquez wrote of having “some mental health issues” and being rejected by women. In a written statement, the Vazquez family said Caleb Vazquez was on the autism spectrum and had grown to resent parts of his identity. The family said they believed that, combined with exposure to hateful rhetoric online, contributed to his radicalization.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Govt slammed an award by the “illegally constituted so-called Court of Arbitration (CoA)” concerning interim measures and status of the Indus Waters Treaty, recalling India’s position that the court has no jurisdiction to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions. India had responded similarly to another award issued by the court in May this year.On this occasion though, according to a Reuters report from Amsterdam, the Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague said that India must uphold the Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan and must also limit work on an hydroelectric plant it is building in J&K.Govt maintains that this court was created in violation of the 1960 IWT which in any case has been put in abeyance by India because of Pakistan’s support to cross-border terrorism.“Today, the illegally constituted so-called Court of Arbitration has issued what it termed as an award concerning Interim Measures and Status of the Indus Waters Treaty. This so-called court was constituted by World Bank in patent breach of terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body,” MEA said.The ministry said that India has never recognised the existence in law of this illegally-constituted and so-called Court of Arbitration, and has consistently maintained that the very establishment of this alleged arbitral body constitutes a grave violation of the Indus Waters Treaty.“Accordingly, India has never appeared before this body and has refused to take any cognisance of its earlier pronouncements,” it said, adding that the court’s awards, now or in the future, will have no effect on India’s actions in connection with the projects being undertaken by India. The MEA also reiterated India’s decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force.The Permanent Court of Arbitration said the Indus Water Treaty remained fully in force, as India had no justification for ending or suspending the agreement.“India must observe its obligations under the Treaty, including those relating to the design and operation of its hydro-electric projects on the Western Rivers,” the intergovernmental court said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Dale ‘Grey Beard’ Sanders, 91, reclaims record as oldest hiker to complete the Appalachian Trail
articles.summary: At 91, Dale Sanders has become the oldest hiker to complete the Appalachian Trail, trekking 2,193 miles from West Virginia to Maine.
articles.body: MILLINOCKET, Maine — More than 14 million older adults fall every year in the U.S., perhaps none so often as 91-year-old Dale Sanders. By his count, Sanders fell 71 times while reclaiming his record as the oldest hiker to complete the Appalachian Trail. Six were what he calls hard falls, including one that led to a brief hospitalization and another just 200 yards from the finish. But none were enough to permanently divert him from the 2,193-mile trail that runs between Springer Mountain in Georgia and Mount Katahdin in Maine. The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines a thru-hike as completing all of the trail’s sections in any order within a year, allowing for pauses. Sanders started Sept. 6 in West Virginia, hopscotched around with some brief breaks and finished Monday atop Maine’s highest peak, where he paused to pray at the sign marking the summit. “I had to thank God, and I had to thank my support team and everybody that got me here,” he said. A long-planned comeback Sanders, whose trail name is Grey Beard, first set the Appalachian Trail record in 2017 at age 82. Four years later, his 83-year-old friend M.J. Eberhart, aka Nimblewill Nomad, took the title. But within months, Sanders announced his comeback plan. While Sanders’ first journey was easier than he expected, the latest was considerably harder. Despite six months of training, he said he wasn’t in the best condition when he returned to the trail. “And even today, I feel that I should probably be in better shape than I am,” he said last month. “But I just have to always go back and say, ‘But I am 91, so I’m blazing new ground hiking long distances like this.’” In June, Sanders was descending Killington Mountain in central Vermont when he fell forward in a boulder field, scraping his legs, arms and hands. “Thank God nothing got broken, but I was banged up,” he said. “I didn’t rub the blood off, I just kept hiking.” Weeks later, his left arm went numb and he ended up at a Maine hospital. What doctors initially feared was a stroke turned out to be a pinched nerve, but though he was soon cleared to resume hiking, he considered giving up. He returned home to Tennessee in early August to be with his wife, whose mother had just died, and she convinced him to press on. His mission changed along the way Some of Sanders’ best days were in Pennsylvania, where he enjoyed well-maintained trails and treats delivered by “trail angels.” “When people are taking care of you and bringing you caramel frappes on the trail, the rocks don’t matter,” he said. In fact, Sanders has become something of a star among fellow hikers. Thousands more follow him on social media, which surprised Sanders and caused him to expand his mission beyond reclaiming his record. “I wanna get it back, but right now, that’s secondary,” he said. “Right now, what’s the most important thing - and it’s one of the things that surprised me – is that people are motivated and given encouragement by my efforts.” Meredith Ewenson, who met Sanders in June while leading a hike in New Hampshire for 10 other women, said he embodied not just the idea that anything is possible, but that the journey matters most. “Seeing it in real life is something that I’ll definitely remember forever,” she said. Ewenson said her group spotted Sanders early in the morning, but it wasn’t until he blazed by them hours later that they saw the Grey Beard logo on his T-shirt and realized who he was. They caught up with him that night at an Appalachian Mountain Club hut, arriving around 4 p.m. “I got here at noon,” he told them. The next morning, she and others cheered as Sanders performed a “victory dance” before setting off again. “My first thought was ‘Wow, his mobility is insane,’” Ewenson said. “His face on that body just doesn’t make any sense. My brain couldn’t compute how he was so impossibly fit for being that age.” Off-trail adventures Sanders was born in Kentucky in 1935, two years before the Appalachian Trail was completed. Bullied as a child for his small size, he gained confidence in solo sports like acrobatics and swimming. He later served in the Navy and retired in 2002 after a long career in parks and recreation. Sanders holds numerous other age-related records, including becoming the oldest person to paddle the entire length of the Mississippi River, an 87-day trip he started on his 87th birthday. On his latest adventure, he tackled obstacles like downed trees or steep scrambles with vigor, though he started to get a bit wobbly toward the end of one 12-mile day. He laid down on the trail, said he needed a power nap and briefly fell asleep. Two minutes later, he got up and kept hiking.

articles.title: “The verdict shouldn’t even take 17 minutes”: YouTuber Matt Walsh calls Lindsay Clancy jury delay a ‘total travesty’ as deliberations continue
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Matt Walsh has reacted strongly to the jury taking hours to reach a verdict in the Lindsay Clancy trial, calling the delay a “total travesty.” The jur.
articles.body: Matt Walsh has reacted strongly to the jury taking hours to reach a verdict in the Lindsay Clancy trial, calling the delay a “total travesty.” The jury had spent about 17 hours deliberating by Monday, August 31, without reaching a decision in the Massachusetts case. Clancy is accused of killing her three children, Cora, Dawson and Callan, in January 2023. She has admitted strangling the children but pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility. Her defense says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors say she planned the killings.Matt Walsh reacts to Lindsay Clancy jury deliberationsWalsh, a host at The Daily Wire and a YouTuber, has repeatedly rejected the insanity defense during the trial. On August 31, after reports said the jury had spent nearly 17 hours deliberating, he wrote on X: “Total travesty. It’s the simplest case imaginable. She murdered three children. The end. The verdict shouldn’t even take 17 minutes, let alone 17 hours.”He had made a similar argument days earlier, questioning why the jury had not reached a decision. On August 28, Walsh wrote: “Seems like not a good sign that there’s no verdict yet. This is a very simple case. Did Lindsay Clancy intentionally murder her children? Yes. Did she plan it out ahead of time? Yes. That’s really all you need to know. First degree murder. Should take a jury of sane people about 10 minutes to reach a conclusion.”Walsh has also focused on the prosecution’s claim that Clancy made choices before the killings that showed planning. He has argued that sending her husband away and then killing the children does not fit his view of an insanity defense. On August 21, he wrote: “Lindsay Clancy had a ‘psychotic break.’ Which is why she planned the murder, researched her plan on Google, sent her husband away from the house, and then methodically executed her children over the course of several minutes. I never knew that you could plan your psychotic break like that.”His comments have been much harsher than the language used by the court. On August 27, he also wrote: “The ‘insanity’ argument for Lindsay Clancy is just this: 1) She had the thought and desire to strangle her children to death. 2) Only an insane person would have those thoughts and desires.
